\chapter{Me and Te --- The Two People Talking}
\label{ch:pronoun-me-te}
\hlchaptermodality{85}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say te quiero and me quieres, and tell the doer form apart from the object form.}

Complete ES-C42-te: produce te quiero and me quieres, and name the English pair that matches tu and te.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[me quieres]{me quieres — \textquotedblleft{}you love me\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C42-me-objeto}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}my name is.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Me llamo}.) That \emph{me} has been in your mouth for more than fifty chapters. This chapter gives it nothing new to look like — only something new to do.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same word, a simpler job}]
In \emph{me llamo}, the \emph{me} points back at the speaker: \emph{I call \textbf{myself}}. That is a special use, and it was the one you needed first.

Here is the ordinary one:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Me} quieres.} — You love \textbf{me}.
\end{quote}

Now \emph{me} is not pointing back at anybody. It is simply the person the verb lands on — the same job \emph{lo} does for a book and \emph{la} does for a meal.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Lo tengo.} — I have it. \emph{Me quieres.} — You love me.
\end{quote}

Same slot, in front of the verb. Same kind of work. The only difference is that \emph{me} is a person and \emph{lo} is a thing, which is a fact about the world rather than a fact about Spanish.

Notice what this chapter did \textbf{not} ask you to learn: a form. You already had it. Some of the ground you gain in a language is like this — not new material, but an old piece turning out to reach further than you were told.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Me} comes from Latin \textbf{mē}, and Latin got it from something far older. English \textbf{me} is not a translation of it and not a borrowing from it — the two are the \textbf{same inherited word}, sitting in two languages that split thousands of years ago and never bothered to change it.

Words this short and this used are the ones that survive intact. That is why your very first Spanish pronoun was also the easiest one you will ever meet.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me llamo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}me quieres\textquotedblright{} — the same syllable, two jobs
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lo tengo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}me quieres\textquotedblright{} — hear that the slot never moves
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}you love me.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Me quieres}}.) Where did the pronoun go? (\textbf{Before} the verb, as always.) Next: the answering half of that sentence.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[te quiero]{te quiero — \textquotedblleft{}I love you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C42-te}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}you love me.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Me quieres}.) Now turn it around in your head: what would \textquotedblleft{}I love you\textquotedblright{} need?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the partner of tú}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{te} — \emph{you}, when you are the one it happens to.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Te quiero.}} — I love you.
\end{quote}

\emph{Tú} is for the one doing; \emph{te} is for the one it lands on. Spanish keeps those apart with two different shapes, the same way it keeps \emph{el} and \emph{lo} apart, and the same way English keeps \emph{I} and \emph{me} apart.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Me quieres.} — You love me. \emph{Te quiero.} — I love you.
\end{quote}

Two words each, and a complete exchange. Read them aloud one after the other: the pair is a conversation.

\textbf{One thing worth knowing before you use it.} \emph{Querer} means \emph{to want}, and you have been using it that way for a long time. But \emph{querer} pointed at a \textbf{person} does not mean wanting them — it means \textbf{loving} them. \emph{Quiero un libro} is \textquotedblleft{}I want a book\textquotedblright{}; \emph{te quiero} is \textquotedblleft{}I love you.\textquotedblright{}

So the sentence is built entirely out of pieces you already had. What is new is not a form — it is that the verb changes its meaning depending on whether its object is a thing or a person.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te quiero\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Me quieres\textquotedblright{} — a whole exchange in four words
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tú\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}te\textquotedblright{}, and hear which one is doing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I love you.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Te quiero}}.) And \textquotedblleft{}you love me.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Me quieres}}.) Next: where \emph{te} came from, and the English word that is the very same one.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[te]{te — the pair English used to have}

\label{lesson:ES-C42-te-thee}



\begin{quote}
Two shapes for one person: \emph{tú} when they act, \emph{te} when it lands on them.

English once had exactly the same two shapes, and they are the same two words.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Te} is Latin \textbf{tē} — the object form of \textbf{tū}, which you already have.

Old English had \textbf{thou} for the doer and \textbf{thee} for the one it happened to. Here is the striking part: \emph{tú}/\emph{te} and \emph{thou}/\emph{thee} are not merely similar. They are \textbf{one ancient pair, inherited twice} — once down the Latin line into Spanish, once down the Germanic line into English.

English later dropped both and let \emph{you} cover the two jobs. Spanish kept them apart, which is why you have two words to learn where a speaker of English feels there should be one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}tú\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}te\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}thou\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}thee\textquotedblright{} — the same split twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English pair matches \emph{tú} and \emph{te}? (\textbf{Thou} and \textbf{thee}.) And which of the two means \textquotedblleft{}the one it happened to\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Te}} — and \emph{thee}.) Next: all four object pronouns in one place, for the first time.
\end{tcolorbox}
